answers.label: Benefits and challenges of consequential methods
answers.text:
PowerOptions supports the development of consequential accounting methods for electricity-sector actions as a complement to Scope 2 attributional accounting. A clear and credible consequential framework has the potential to improve decision usefulness by distinguishing between emissions associated with electricity consumption and the system-wide emissions impacts of electricity procurement and investment decisions.

Consequential accounting can help address an important gap in current reporting frameworks. Many organizations face structural, regulatory, or cost constraints that limit their ability to procure deliverable renewable electricity or to align procurement directly with the times and locations of consumption. In these circumstances, organizations may pursue actions specifically intended to deliver greater system-level emissions reductions, including investments in new renewable generation in higher-emitting regions. Recognition of these actions through a consequential framework can help ensure that reporting better reflects the intent and impact of electricity-sector actions, without conflating them with attributional inventories.

In practice, PowerOptions has supported Members in evaluating electricity procurement opportunities using grid emissions intensity as one of several criteria, particularly when assessing projects intended to deliver system-level emissions reductions rather than to serve deliverable load. In several cases, analysis demonstrated that developing renewable projects in regions with higher marginal emissions was expected to deliver greater emissions reductions than siting equivalent projects in New England, where grid emissions are already comparatively low. A consequential accounting framework that can transparently recognize this type of decision-making would improve alignment between reported outcomes and emissions-reduction intent.

At the same time, consequential accounting presents important challenges. These methods can be data-intensive, sensitive to modeling assumptions, and difficult to apply consistently across regions. Excessive methodological complexity or highly granular data requirements could limit feasibility for nonprofits, public entities, and aggregated buyers, reducing participation and comparability. Clear distinctions between consequential claims and Scope 2 inventory claims are therefore essential to avoid confusion or double counting.

Unintended consequences should also be carefully avoided. If consequential accounting is positioned as a substitute for, or justification to narrow, Scope 2 market-based accounting, it could discourage long-term contracting and aggregated procurement strategies that have historically supported new renewable generation. Consequential accounting should instead be developed as a parallel, clearly labeled framework that recognizes system-level impacts while preserving the integrity, accessibility, and real-world effectiveness of Scope 2 accounting.
